sections.title: The Gateway: Why do a few hours of moving light in a dark room change the way we see our lives?
sections.html:
Web address: /movies/why-we-love-movies/ · Keywords: history of cinema for beginners, how movies began, why we love movies, cinema explained

The lights go down. A hundred strangers stop talking. For two hours, they laugh at the same joke, hold their breath at the same moment and walk out a little changed. Nothing in that room was real, and yet everyone felt something real.

This short course follows one question, why do movies have such power over us?, in twelve small steps: from storytellers around a fire to the Lumière brothers, from Dadasaheb Phalke to streaming and AI. Each page answers one question in about two minutes and hands you the next one. You can stop after any page and still leave with a complete answer.

By the end you will be able to:

  • Tell the story of cinema in order, from shadow puppets to streaming.
  • Explain why a row of still pictures looks like motion.
  • Say how Indian cinema began and why it sings.
  • Explain, with real ideas from India and the world, why we cry for people who do not exist.
  • Read box-office numbers without being fooled by them.

sections.title: What did people do for stories before the movies?
sections.html:
Short answer: They gathered around storytellers, theatres, puppet shows and "magic lanterns". Cinema did not invent the human hunger for stories; it gave that hunger a new machine.

Keywords: entertainment before cinema, shadow puppets history, magic lantern, kathputli, history of storytelling

Stories around the fire

For most of human history, the movie screen was a face lit by fire. Storytellers carried epics in their memory. In India, kathakars, bhopas with their painted phad scrolls in Rajasthan, and singers of the Alha and Pabuji epics travelled from village to village. Their audiences knew the story already and came anyway, for the telling.

Theatre: the first "big screen"

Theatre gave stories a stage, costumes and an audience in rows. Bharata's Natyashastra (compiled roughly 200 BCE to 200 CE) is one of the oldest books on drama in the world, and Greek tragedy in Athens is of similar antiquity. Both understood something movies would later use: a crowd feels more together than alone.

Light and shadow

Long before electricity, people were already telling stories with light. Shadow puppets danced in India (tholu bommalata in Andhra Pradesh, togalu gombeyaata in Karnataka), in Indonesia (wayang kulit), in China and in Turkey (Karagöz). Rajasthan's kathputli used strings instead of shadows.

From the 1600s, the magic lantern projected painted glass slides onto a wall; it is usually credited to the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens around 1659. Showmen used moving slides, smoke and sound effects to make audiences scream at ghosts.

So what was missing?

Real motion. Every one of these arts could show a picture, or a performer moving live. None could capture a real moment and play it back. That was the dream of the 1800s.

Remember this: Movies are the newest member of a very old family: the storyteller, the stage and the shadow on the wall.

Next: So who first caught a real moment on film, and did audiences really run from a train?

sections.title: Who made the first movie, and did audiences really run from a train?
sections.html:
Short answer: The oldest surviving motion picture is Louis Le Prince's Roundhay Garden Scene (1888). Cinema as a public show began with the Lumière brothers' paid screening in Paris on 28 December 1895. The famous story of people running from a train is most likely a legend.

Keywords: first movie ever made, Lumière brothers, Roundhay Garden Scene, Edison kinetoscope, train panic myth

Many inventors, one race

In the 1880s and 1890s, inventors in France, Britain, the USA and Germany all raced to capture motion. Eadweard Muybridge photographed a galloping horse with a row of cameras in 1878. Louis Le Prince filmed a few seconds of people walking in a garden in Leeds in 1888. Thomas Edison's team, led by William Kennedy Laurie Dickson, built the Kinetoscope, a peep-show box for one viewer at a time (public from 1894).

The night cinema was born

Auguste and Louis Lumière built the Cinématographe, a camera that was also a projector. On 28 December 1895, in the Salon Indien of the Grand Café in Paris, they showed about ten short films to a paying audience. One showed workers leaving their factory. Life itself had become a show.

The train that did not attack

The Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat is famous for making audiences flee. Film historians have found no reliable report of such a panic, and the film was not part of the first programme. The legend survived because it says something true: people had never seen anything like it.

From records to dreams

A magician named Georges Méliès saw the show and understood it could do more than record. His A Trip to the Moon (1902) used tricks, sets and stop-motion to make the impossible visible. Cinema now had two paths: the Lumières' real world and Méliès' dream world. Every film since walks one of them, or both.

Remember this: Cinema has no single inventor. It was born from many hands, and became an art the moment someone used it to tell a story.

sections.title: Why does a row of still pictures look like it is moving?
sections.html:
Short answer: Your brain fills the gaps. When still images that differ slightly flash by fast enough, the visual system reads them as smooth motion. The old explanation, "persistence of vision", is now considered incomplete.

Keywords: how do movies work, frames per second, persistence of vision myth, phi phenomenon, 24 fps

A trick played by your brain

A film is a series of still frames. Show them fast and your brain stops seeing separate pictures and starts seeing a moving world. Psychologists call related effects apparent motion (the phi phenomenon and beta movement, studied by Max Wertheimer in 1912). The brain has motion detectors that respond to change between images, and they happily accept a well-timed series of stills.

Why "persistence of vision" is not the full story

Many textbooks still say an image "stays on the retina" and blends with the next. Lingering images do help hide the dark gap between frames, but they would produce a blur, not motion. The motion itself is built by the brain.

How fast is fast enough?

Silent films ran at around 16 to 20 frames per second, often varied by hand. With sound, speed had to be fixed so voices would not change pitch, and 24 frames per second became the standard in the late 1920s. Projectors flash each frame two or three times, so the light flickers 48 or 72 times a second, too fast for most eyes to notice. Peter Jackson's The Hobbit (2012) tried 48 frames per second; many viewers felt it looked "too real", which shows how much our taste is trained by habit.

The pictures before the movies

Toys like the zoetrope and the phenakistiscope (1830s) proved the effect decades before film. Spin a drum of drawings, look through the slits, and a horse runs.

Remember this: Motion in the movies lives in your head. The screen gives the brain clues; the brain makes the magic.

Next: Within months of Paris, those flickering pictures reached Bombay. How did India get its first film?

sections.title: How did India get its first film?
sections.html:
Short answer: The Lumière films were shown in Bombay on 7 July 1896. Dadasaheb Phalke's Raja Harishchandra, released on 3 May 1913, is generally regarded as India's first full-length feature film.

Keywords: first Indian film, Raja Harishchandra, Dadasaheb Phalke, Alam Ara first talkie, history of Indian cinema

Cinema arrives by ship

Barely six months after Paris, the Lumière agents showed their films at Watson's Hotel in Bombay on 7 July 1896. Indians soon picked up cameras: Harishchandra Sakharam Bhatavdekar ("Save Dada") filmed a wrestling match in Bombay in 1899, one of the first films shot by an Indian.

A printer who saw Christ on screen

Dhundiraj Govind Phalke was a printer and photographer. In 1910 he watched The Life of Christ and asked: why not Indian gods and heroes on screen? He went to London to learn, bought equipment, and filmed the story of the truthful king Harishchandra. No woman from a "respectable" family would act then, so a young man, Anna Salunke, played the queen Taramati. Raja Harishchandra opened at the Coronation Cinema, Bombay, on 3 May 1913. (Some historians point to Shree Pundalik, 1912, as an earlier contender; it is usually treated as a filmed play.)

Mythology first, then everything

Early Indian films drew on the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Puranas, because audiences already loved those stories from theatre and katha. The South followed with Keechaka Vadham (1918), Bengal with Madan Theatres' productions, and soon studios rose in Bombay, Calcutta, Kolhapur, Pune and Madras.

The day India spoke

On 14 March 1931, Ardeshir Irani's Alam Ara became India's first talkie. Within a year, films spoke Tamil, Telugu, Bengali and Marathi. Sound turned one Indian cinema into many: the birth of the language industries you will meet in Part 1.

Remember this: Indian cinema began with a printer's dream and a myth everyone knew. India now certifies more feature films each year than any other country.

Next: Before 1927, films everywhere had no recorded sound. So why do historians say silent films were never silent?

sections.title: Why were silent films never silent?
sections.html:
Short answer: Because almost every screening had live sound: a pianist, an organ, a full orchestra or, in Japan, a narrator called a benshi. The films had no recorded dialogue, but the cinema hall was full of music.

Keywords: silent film music, what is a benshi, Charlie Chaplin silent films, intertitles, silent era

The music in the room

In big city cinemas of the 1910s and 1920s, orchestras played scores written or arranged for the film. Smaller halls had a single pianist who improvised to the mood: chase music, love music, danger music. Cinema organs were built with drums, bells and bird whistles. In India too, silent shows were accompanied by live musicians, and sometimes by a narrator explaining the story.

The storytellers of Japan

Japan's benshi stood beside the screen and voiced characters, explained scenes and added commentary. Popular benshi were stars, and audiences chose cinemas by who was narrating. Their popularity is one reason Japan kept making silent films well into the 1930s.

Telling a story with the face

Without speech, actors and directors invented a universal language: faces, bodies and editing. Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton and Harold Lloyd made comedy that needs no translation even today. Short written cards called intertitles gave dialogue or explanations, and could be swapped for any language, which made silent films easy to sell around the world.

An art that peaked and vanished

By the late 1920s, films such as F. W. Murnau's Sunrise (1927) and Carl Theodor Dreyer's The Passion of Joan of Arc (1928) showed how far the silent art had grown. Then, within about three years, it was nearly gone. Sadly, most silent films are lost: the Library of Congress estimates that around 75 percent of American silent features no longer survive, and only a few fragments of India's roughly 1,300 silent films remain.

Remember this: Silent cinema was a complete art of music, gesture and image, and it taught the world a shared language of the screen.

Next: Then the movies learned to talk. What did they gain, and what did they lose?

sections.title: What changed when movies learned to talk?
sections.html:
Short answer: Sound arrived with The Jazz Singer (1927) and changed everything within a few years: acting, cameras, music, careers and, above all, language. In India, sound gave birth to film songs and to separate regional industries.

Keywords: first sound film, The Jazz Singer, talkies history, Alam Ara songs, why Indian films have songs

"You ain't heard nothin' yet"

Warner Bros. released The Jazz Singer in October 1927 using the Vitaphone system, which played sound from a disc in time with the film. Only parts of it had synchronised speech and song, but audiences were thrilled. By 1930, Hollywood had mostly stopped making silent films.

What was lost for a while

Early microphones were weak, so cameras were locked inside soundproof booths and actors had to stand near hidden microphones. Films became stiff for a few years. Some stars with voices or accents audiences disliked lost their careers. (The musical Singin' in the Rain, 1952, jokes about exactly this.) Soon cameras learned to move again, and sound became a new tool: the creak of a door, a silence before a gunshot.

Why India sings

Alam Ara (1931) had seven songs. Indian audiences came from a theatre tradition, from Parsi theatre to Sangeet Natak to folk forms, in which music and drama were one. So songs became the heart of Indian cinema, and playback singing (singers recording songs that actors lip-sync) became standard from the mid-1930s. Even today, a film's songs often reach people before the film does.

One cinema becomes many

Silent films could swap their intertitles for any language. Talkies could not. So sound split cinema along language lines everywhere. In India, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Marathi and later Kannada, Malayalam and other industries grew their own studios, stars and styles.

Remember this: Sound gave films a voice, and gave every language its own cinema.

Next: Talking pictures made us laugh and weep. But why do we cry for people who never existed?

sections.title: Why do we cry for people who do not exist?
sections.html:
Short answer: Because the brain responds to stories much as it responds to real people, and because a film gives us emotion in a safe frame. Indian aesthetics calls this tasting of emotion "rasa"; Aristotle called its cleansing effect "catharsis".

Keywords: why do we cry at movies, rasa theory explained, catharsis, psychology of film, paradox of fiction

The puzzle

You know the hero is an actor. You know the music was added later. You cry anyway. Philosophers call this the paradox of fiction (the philosopher Colin Radford asked it sharply in 1975): how can we feel real emotions for what we know is unreal?

What the brain does

When we watch a character, we read faces, follow goals and predict danger, using the same social skills we use with real people. Brain-imaging studies show that watching emotions activates regions also involved in feeling them. Research by Paul Zak's team has linked emotionally gripping stories to a rise in oxytocin, a hormone tied to empathy, though such results are still debated. The short version: the brain does not fully switch off its caring system just because the person is fictional.

Rasa: India's answer, 2,000 years old

The Natyashastra says a performance creates rasa, a "taste" of emotion that the audience savours. We do not suffer the hero's grief; we taste karuna (compassion) in a refined, shared form. Classical writers listed eight rasas, and later thinkers such as Abhinavagupta added shanta (peace), making the famous navarasa. A good Indian "masala" film often tries to serve many rasas in one sitting, like a thali.

Catharsis and safety

Aristotle wrote that tragedy arouses pity and fear and brings their catharsis, a release or cleansing. Psychologists today add that films give us a safe rehearsal: we feel loss, fear or love without the real cost, and practise feeling for others.

The editing trick

In the 1920s, Soviet filmmaker Lev Kuleshov reportedly showed the same neutral face after shots of soup, a coffin and a child, and viewers "saw" hunger, grief and joy. This Kuleshov effect shows that much of the emotion is built by us.

Remember this: Movies borrow the brain's machinery for caring about people, and give it a safe space to feel.

sections.title: How did movies become the world's biggest dream factory?
sections.html:
Short answer: Through studios and stars. From the 1910s, studios in Hollywood, Bombay, Madras, Tokyo and elsewhere made films like a factory makes cars, on a schedule, with salaried stars. That system made cinema the dominant popular art of the 20th century.

Keywords: Hollywood studio system, star system, Bombay Talkies, Prabhat studio, why is it called Hollywood

Why Hollywood?

American filmmakers moved west to Los Angeles in the 1910s for sunshine, varied landscapes and distance from Edison's patent company in the East. By the 1920s, Hollywood was the capital of world cinema.

The studio system

From about 1920 to 1950, five big studios (MGM, Paramount, Warner Bros., 20th Century-Fox and RKO) owned everything: writers, stars on long contracts, sound stages and even the cinemas. In 1948, the US Supreme Court's Paramount decision forced them to sell their cinemas, and the old system began to break.

India's studios

India built its own dream factories: Prabhat (Kolhapur, later Pune), New Theatres (Calcutta), Bombay Talkies, Gemini and AVM (Madras), Vauhini and Vijaya in the Telugu world. Actors, musicians and writers were on monthly salaries. After independence, independent producers and the star system took over.

The star system

Studios learned that people come to see someone. Stars became brands, from Charlie Chaplin and Greta Garbo to Raj Kapoor, Dilip Kumar, M. G. Ramachandran, N. T. Rama Rao, Rajkumar, Uttam Kumar, Amitabh Bachchan and Rajinikanth. In South India, film stars even became chief ministers: M. G. Ramachandran and J. Jayalalithaa in Tamil Nadu, N. T. Rama Rao in Andhra Pradesh.

How big is it now?

India certifies more feature films in a year than any other country, usually well over 1,500 (CBFC annual reports), and Nigeria's Nollywood is second or third by volume (UNESCO data). The USA still earns the most money worldwide.

Remember this: Studios turned dreams into a product and stars into family members of millions.

Next: Yet Hollywood, Bollywood, Seoul and Tehran make films that feel totally different. Why?

sections.title: Why does every country make its films differently?
sections.html:
Short answer: Because films grow out of a country's language, history, money, censorship and taste in storytelling. Indian films serve many emotions with songs; Hollywood loves tight plots; Iranian and Italian masters found poetry in everyday life.

Keywords: world cinema explained, difference between Bollywood and Hollywood, Italian neorealism, Iranian cinema, Nollywood

Taste in stories

A typical Indian popular film runs longer, mixes action, comedy, romance and tears, and pauses for songs, because it grew from theatre and the navarasa idea (MOV-00.07). Hollywood screenwriting manuals teach a tight three-act structure around one goal. Neither is "right"; they are different meals.

History leaves fingerprints

After the Second World War, Italian directors with no money and ruined studios filmed on real streets with non-actors: Italian neorealism (Bicycle Thieves, 1948). It inspired Satyajit Ray to make Pather Panchali (1955). In the 1950s and 1960s, French critics who became directors broke the rules of editing: the French New Wave.

Limits that sparked creativity

Iranian filmmakers worked under strict censorship and often turned to children, landscapes and small moral stories; Abbas Kiarostami's Taste of Cherry won the Palme d'Or in 1997. Danish directors wrote themselves strict rules in the Dogme 95 manifesto to escape big-budget habits.

Money shapes form

Nigeria's Nollywood grew from home-video tapes after Living in Bondage (1992): fast, cheap and close to its audience. South Korea built the "Korean wave" with screen quotas, investment and fearless genre films, leading to Parasite winning the Best Picture Oscar in 2020, the first non-English-language film to do so.

Language and market

A Malayalam film speaks to about 35 million native speakers; a Hindi or English film to hundreds of millions. That affects budgets, themes and risk-taking, and helps explain why smaller industries often surprise us with bold, realistic stories.

Remember this: Every cinema is a mirror of its people, shaped by what they love, what they have lived through and what they are allowed to say.

sections.title: Did television, video and streaming try to kill the cinema?
sections.html:
Short answer: Each new screen was expected to kill cinema, and each time cinema changed instead: widescreen and colour against television, multiplexes against video, event films against streaming. Theatres shrank, but the habit of watching together survived.

Keywords: did TV kill cinema, CinemaScope history, VHS and movies, multiplex in India, streaming vs theatres

Round one: television (1950s)

As American families bought televisions, cinema attendance fell sharply. Hollywood fought back with what a small black-and-white box could not give: colour, widescreen (CinemaScope, launched with The Robe, 1953), 3D glasses and huge epics such as Ben-Hur (1959). In India, television spread later, in the 1980s, with Doordarshan's Ramayan (1987) emptying streets on Sunday mornings.

Round two: video (1970s to 1990s)

Videocassettes let people watch films at home and also made piracy easy. In 1984, the US Supreme Court ruled in the "Betamax case" that home recording for personal use was legal. Studios then found that selling tapes was very profitable. In India, the video boom of the 1980s hurt cinemas and audiences moved back with better halls; the first multiplex, PVR Anupam in Delhi (1997), began a new era.

Round three: streaming (2007 onwards)

Netflix began streaming in 2007; then came Amazon Prime Video, Disney+, Hotstar and many more. During the COVID-19 pandemic (2020 to 2021), cinemas closed and many films went straight to streaming. Some people predicted the end of theatres. Instead, big "event" films returned audiences to halls, and films such as RRR and Oppenheimer became shared experiences again.

What survives

Each round killed something (the newsreel, the single-screen village theatre, the DVD shop) and kept the core: a story, a dark room and people feeling it together.

Remember this: New screens do not kill old ones; they force them to discover what only they can do.

sections.title: How much money does a movie really make?
sections.html:
Short answer: Less than the headline number. "Box office" usually means gross ticket sales, of which cinemas keep a large share and taxes take another. Studios also earn from streaming, TV, music and other rights. As checked on 5 October 2026, the highest worldwide gross is Avengers: Endgame (about US$2.93 billion after a 2026 re-release), just ahead of Avatar.

Keywords: highest grossing movie of all time, box office explained, gross vs net collection, Indian box office, film budget

Gross, net and share

Gross is the total value of tickets sold. In India, trade reports also quote net (gross minus GST and local taxes). From the net, the cinema keeps its share, and the rest (the distributor share) goes back toward the producer. A film with a "₹300 crore" headline might return far less to the people who made it.

Budget is only half the cost

A film's production budget does not include marketing, which for a big Hollywood release can equal a large part of the budget. A common rule of thumb is that a theatrical film must earn roughly two to three times its budget at the box office to break even, though every deal is different.

The other money

Indian producers often sell satellite, digital (streaming) and music rights before release, sometimes covering a large share of the cost. Hollywood earns from streaming licences, TV, merchandise and theme parks.

The record holders (as checked on 5 October 2026)

Worldwide, not adjusted for inflation: Avengers: Endgame (2019) about US$2.925 billion, Avatar (2009) about US$2.923 billion, Avatar: The Way of Water (2022), Titanic (1997) and China's Ne Zha 2 (2025), the highest-grossing animated film and non-English-language film (figures: Euronews from Box Office Mojo data). Adjusted for inflation, Gone with the Wind (1939) is usually ranked first (Guinness World Records). In India, Dangal (2016) is the highest-grossing Indian film worldwide, at around ₹2,000 crore, much of it earned in China.

Why numbers mislead

Figures are rarely audited publicly, are reported by interested parties and change with exchange rates and re-releases. That is why this site always gives the source and date.

Remember this: Box office is a scoreboard, not a bank statement. Read it with the source and date.

Next: With streaming, AI and virtual sets, the movies are changing again. What is their future?

sections.title: What is the future of the movies?
sections.html:
Short answer: Movies are moving toward virtual production, AI-assisted tools, global audiences and streaming-first releases, while the big-screen event survives. The open questions are about creativity, jobs and trust, not about whether people will still want stories.

Keywords: future of cinema, AI in filmmaking, virtual production LED volume, pan-Indian films, will cinemas survive

New tools on set

Virtual production uses giant LED screens showing computer-generated backgrounds that move with the camera, popularised by the series The Mandalorian (2019). Directors can shoot a desert or a planet inside a studio, with real light falling on the actors.

AI: helper or threat?

AI can now help with editing, dubbing, de-ageing, visual effects and even generating short clips. In 2023, Hollywood's writers (WGA) and actors (SAG-AFTRA) went on long strikes, in part to win protections against unconsented use of AI and digital replicas. The debate continues worldwide, and India's industry is having it too.

One world, many languages

Subtitles and dubbing on streaming platforms have made language less of a wall. Parasite, RRR, Squid Game (a series) and KPop Demon Hunters (Best Animated Feature at the 2026 Oscars) found global audiences. In India, "pan-Indian" films like Baahubali, K.G.F and Pushpa are released in five or more languages at once. RRR's "Naatu Naatu" won the Oscar for Best Original Song in 2023.

New forms

Interactive films (Black Mirror: Bandersnatch, 2018), virtual reality, vertical "micro-dramas" on phones and games that feel like films are all testing the edges of what a movie is.

The question that remains

Every new technology has changed how we watch. None has changed why. We still want to sit with others in the dark and feel a story together. That is the thread you will follow through the rest of this site.

Remember this: The future of film will be decided less by machines than by whether stories keep earning our trust.

## MOV-00.R Recap: The story of the movies in one page

Keywords: history of cinema summary, cinema quiz, movies for beginners

  1. Cinema joined the oldest human habit: telling stories with voice, stage and shadow.
  2. Many inventors created moving pictures; the Lumières' 1895 screening began cinema as a public show.
  3. Motion on screen is built by your brain from fast still images (24 per second as the standard).
  4. India's first full-length feature was Raja Harishchandra (1913); its first talkie, Alam Ara (1931).
  5. Silent films were full of live music; sound (1927) gave films a voice and split cinema into language industries.
  6. We cry at films because the brain cares about people even in stories; India calls this tasting of emotion rasa.
  7. Studios and stars made cinema a world industry; India makes the most films, the USA earns the most.
  8. Each new screen (TV, video, streaming) changed cinema without ending it.

Test yourself: Who held the first paid screening? Why 24 frames? What is rasa? What is the difference between gross and net? Which was India's first talkie?

parts.title: Film Industries of the World
parts.intro:
About this Part. The first great classification: where films are made. It goes from India to every continent. Each industry has a one- or two-line identity card (language, centre, nickname, first film, signature), its key eras, its legends and a Film Register of landmark films, decade by decade. Nicknames ending in "-wood" are informal; the proper name is given first. The registers are a curated landmark selection, not a complete list: see "How the registers grow" at the end of this Part.
Register fields. Year · Film · Director · Lead cast · Box office / reception · Major awards and why it matters. A dash (—) means not recorded here, never a guess. Box-office figures are approximate, not inflation-adjusted, and carry their source in Part 13.

sections.title: Indian Cinema: one country, more than twenty film languages
sections.html:
Before you start — MOV-01. India is the world's largest film producer by number of films. It is not one industry but a family of language industries that share stars, music and technicians, and increasingly release "pan-Indian" films in many languages at once. Start with Hindi cinema, then the four big southern industries, then the East, West, North-east and the smaller language cinemas. See also: MOV-09 History, MOV-12.1 Indian awards, MUS (film music), BOK (adaptations).

Films in Hindi and Hindustani, centred in Mumbai (Bombay, hence "Bollywood"). Born with Raja Harishchandra (1913) and the talkie Alam Ara (1931); known worldwide for song-and-dance, melodrama, stars and the masala mix of every emotion. Tags: #india #hindi #mumbai #bollywood

  • Silent era (1913–1931): mythologicals and stunts from Phalke's Hindustan Film Company, Kohinoor and Imperial studios.
  • Studio era (1930s–1940s): Bombay Talkies (Himanshu Rai, Devika Rani), Prabhat, Ranjit, Minerva Movietone (Sohrab Modi), Wadia Movietone (Fearless Nadia).
  • Golden age (1947–1960s): social realism and romance of Raj Kapoor, Guru Dutt, Bimal Roy, Mehboob Khan, V. Shantaram; the music of Naushad, S. D. Burman, Shankar–Jaikishan; Lata Mangeshkar and Mohammed Rafi.
  • Colour, romance and Rajesh Khanna (1960s–early 1970s): Kashmir songs, Shammi Kapoor's energy, the first superstar Rajesh Khanna.
  • Angry young man and masala (1973–1980s): Amitabh Bachchan, the writers Salim–Javed, multi-starrers like Sholay.
  • Parallel / New Indian Cinema (1969–1990s): state-funded (FFC, later NFDC) realist cinema: Mrinal Sen (Hindi work), Shyam Benegal, Govind Nihalani, Mani Kaul, Kumar Shahani, Saeed Mirza, Sai Paranjpye.
  • Romance and the NRI era (1989–2000s): Maine Pyar Kiya, DDLJ; Shah Rukh, Salman and Aamir Khan; overseas markets; corporatisation (industry status for film, 2001).
  • Multiplex and new-wave Hindi films (2000s–2010s): Dibakar Banerjee, Anurag Kashyap, Vishal Bhardwaj, Zoya Akhtar, Rajkumar Hirani; small-town stories.
  • Streaming and pan-India (2020s): OTT originals, South-Indian dubbed hits in the Hindi belt, big-event films.
  • Signature elements: playback songs, item numbers, dialogue-baazi, family melodrama, interval twist, censorship by CBFC certificate (U, U/A 7+, 13+, 16+, A, S).

Films in Tamil, centred in Chennai (Kodambakkam, hence "Kollywood"). First talkie Kalidas (1931); deeply tied to Dravidian politics, star cults and bold music. Tags: #india #tamil #chennai #kollywood

  • Silent beginnings: Keechaka Vadham (1918, R. Nataraja Mudaliar), the first South Indian silent feature.
  • Studio era: Gemini (S. S. Vasan), AVM (A. V. Meiyappan), Modern Theatres (Salem).
  • Dravidian film politics: writers C. N. Annadurai and M. Karunanidhi; stars M. G. Ramachandran and J. Jayalalithaa became chief ministers.
  • The great acting traditions: Sivaji Ganesan, Gemini Ganesan, Savitri; later Kamal Haasan and Rajinikanth.
  • Village realism (late 1970s): Bharathiraja, Mahendran, Balu Mahendra.
  • The Mani Ratnam and A. R. Rahman era (1980s–1990s).
  • New-wave Tamil (2000s–): Bala, Vetrimaaran, Pa. Ranjith, Karthik Subbaraj, Lokesh Kanagaraj's "Cinematic Universe".

Films in Telugu, centred in Hyderabad (earlier Madras). Known for mythologicals, larger-than-life heroes and, today, India's biggest pan-Indian spectacles. Tags: #india #telugu #hyderabad #tollywood

  • Beginnings: Bhishma Pratigna (1921, R. S. Prakash) silent; Bhakta Prahlada (1932, H. M. Reddy) usually counted as the first Telugu talkie.
  • Golden age (1950s–1960s): Vijaya and Vauhini studios; N. T. Rama Rao (as Krishna and Rama), Akkineni Nageswara Rao, Savitri, S. V. Ranga Rao.
  • K. Viswanath's music films and the art-house of B. Narsing Rao.
  • Mass-hero era: Chiranjeevi, Balakrishna, Nagarjuna, Venkatesh; then Mahesh Babu, Pawan Kalyan, Allu Arjun, Prabhas, Jr NTR, Ram Charan.
  • Ramoji Film City (1996), among the largest film studio complexes in the world (Guinness World Records).
  • Rajamouli and the pan-Indian wave (2015–).

  • New Generation (2010s–): Lijo Jose Pellissery, Dileesh Pothan, Aashiq Abu; actors Fahadh Faasil, Parvathy Thiruvothu.

Films in Bhojpuri, made mainly in Mumbai and Patna for audiences in Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand and the Bhojpuri diaspora (Mauritius, Fiji, Suriname, Trinidad). First film Ganga Maiyya Tohe Piyari Chadhaibo (1963, Kundan Kumar), encouraged by President Rajendra Prasad. Revived in the 2000s by Sasura Bada Paisawala (2004, Manoj Tiwari). Known for folk music, stars such as Ravi Kishan and Dinesh Lal Yadav "Nirahua", and debates over vulgarity in songs. Tags: #india #bhojpuri #bihar #up

  • Odia (Ollywood): from Bhubaneswar and Cuttack; first film Sita Bibaha (1936, Mohan Sundar Deb Goswami); art-house master Nirad N. Mohapatra (Maya Miriga, 1984).
  • Assamese (Jollywood): from Guwahati; first film Joymoti (1935, Jyoti Prasad Agarwala, made at his own Chitraban studio); Bhabendra Nath Saikia, Jahnu Barua; Rima Das's Village Rockstars (2017) won the National Award and was India's Oscar entry.
  • Manipuri: first feature Matamgi Manipur (1972, Deb Kumar Bose); Aribam Syam Sharma's Imagi Ningthem (1981) won the Grand Prix at the Nantes Three Continents Festival. After armed groups banned Hindi films (2000), Manipur grew its own digital film industry.
  • Khasi, Garo, Mizo, Naga, Kokborok, Bodo and Nepali-language cinemas: small but rising industries; Manik Raitong (1984) was the first Khasi film.
  • Maithili, Magahi, Angika and Santali films: Kanyadan (1965) is often cited as the first Maithili film; Santali cinema is growing in Jharkhand and Odisha.
  • Sikkimese and Darjeeling Nepali-language films (link MOV-04.6 Nepal).

  • Gujarati (Dhollywood): first talkie Narsinh Mehta (1932, Nanubhai Vakil); revival after 2012; Hellaro (2019, Abhishek Shah) won the National Award for Best Feature Film; Pan Nalin's Last Film Show (Chhello Show, 2021) was India's Oscar entry and made the shortlist.
  • Punjabi (Pollywood): from Mohali, Chandigarh and Lahore before Partition; Sheela (Pind di Kudi, 1935) among the first; Chann Pardesi (1980) won a National Award; boom since Jatt & Juliet (2012) and Carry On Jatta (2012); stars Diljit Dosanjh, Gippy Grewal, Ammy Virk; huge Canadian diaspora market.
  • Rajasthani: first film Nazrana (1942); hits such as Bai Chali Sasariye (1988); small but loved, with Marwari, Mewari and Hadoti dialects.
  • Haryanvi: Chandrawal (1984) was a landmark rural hit; now growing on YouTube and streaming.
  • Garhwali and Kumaoni (Uttarakhand): Jagwal (1983, Parashar Gaur) is regarded as the first Garhwali film.
  • Kashmiri, Dogri and Ladakhi: Mehjoor (1964) is often cited as the first Kashmiri film.
  • Chhattisgarhi (Chhollywood): Kahi Debe Sandesh (1965, Manu Nayak) was the first; revived after 2000 with Mor Chhainha Bhuinya.
  • Konkani: Mogacho Anvddo (1950, Jerry Braganza); Nachom-ia Kumpasar (2014) a modern classic.
  • Sindhi: Abana (1958) in India; Sindhi films also in Pakistan.
  • Sanskrit: Adi Shankaracharya (1983, G. V. Iyer) was the first Sanskrit feature and won the National Award for Best Feature Film.

  • Tulu (Coastalwood): from Mangaluru and Udupi; first film Enna Thangadi (1971); Kantara's world grew from this coast.
  • Kodava: from Kodagu (Coorg); Naada Mann Naada Koota (1972) is cited as the first.
  • Beary, Badaga, Irula and other community-language films: Byari (2011) won the National Award for Best Feature Film.

  • Documentary: Films Division (1948–2022, merged into NFDC), Anand Patwardhan, Deepa Dhanraj, the Oscar-winning short The Elephant Whisperers (2022, Kartiki Gonsalves, produced by Guneet Monga; Oscar 2023); Writing with Fire (Oscar-nominated, 2022); All That Breathes (Shaunak Sen; Cannes L'Œil d'or 2022).
  • Animation: Ek Anek Aur Ekta (1974, Doordarshan short), Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama (1992, Indo-Japanese), Hanuman (2005), Mahavatar Narsimha (2025); Indian studios in global VFX (Prime Focus/DNEG, Red Chillies VFX).
  • Independent and festival cinema: Payal Kapadia, Chaitanya Tamhane, Rima Das, Pan Nalin, Amit Masurkar, Kanu Behl; film institutes FTII (Pune, 1960) and SRFTI (Kolkata, 1995).
  • Short films and YouTube cinema: a nursery for new talent in every language.

sections.title: Cinema of the Americas
sections.html:
Before you start — MOV-02. From Hollywood, the most powerful film industry in history, to the Golden Age of Mexico, Brazil's Cinema Novo and Argentina's new cinema. See also: MOV-10.1 Oscars, MOV-09.4 Studio era, MOV-08 Movements.

The American film industry, centred in Los Angeles since the 1910s, the world's largest by revenue. Known for the studio and star systems, genre storytelling, blockbusters, franchises and global distribution. Tags: #usa #english #hollywood

  • The Big Five and Little Three (1920s–1948): MGM, Paramount, Warner Bros., 20th Century-Fox, RKO; Universal, Columbia, United Artists.
  • Classical Hollywood (1927–1960): invisible editing, three-act stories, the Production Code (1934–1968).
  • New Hollywood (1967–1980): Coppola, Scorsese, Spielberg, Lucas, Altman; the director as author.
  • Blockbuster era (1975–): Jaws (1975) and Star Wars (1977) created the summer blockbuster.
  • Franchises and cinematic universes (2008–): Marvel Cinematic Universe, DC, Pixar, Disney.
  • Streaming studios: Netflix, Amazon MGM, Apple, now major producers.

Sub-industries and centres of American film

  • American independent cinema: Sundance, Miramax, A24, Neon; John Cassavetes to the Safdie brothers.
  • New York cinema: Woody Allen, Spike Lee, Martin Scorsese's city films.
  • Georgia / Atlanta ("Y'allywood"): a production hub since tax incentives of 2008.
  • African-American cinema: Oscar Micheaux's "race films" (1919–), Blaxploitation (1970s), Spike Lee, Ava DuVernay, Jordan Peele, Ryan Coogler.
  • Hispanic and Latino American film, Asian-American film (Everything Everywhere All at Once, 2022), Native American film (Smoke Signals, 1998).
  • Faith-based, Christian films and the Utah-based Latter-day Saint film scene.
  • Animation studios: Disney, Pixar, DreamWorks, Laika, Sony Pictures Animation.

sections.title: Cinema of Europe
sections.html:
Before you start — MOV-03. Europe gave the world the first film shows and most of the great film movements. Learn each country's industry here and the movements in Part 3. See also: MOV-11 Festivals (Cannes, Venice, Berlin), MOV-08 Movements.

The birthplace of public cinema (Lumière, Méliès, Pathé and Gaumont, the world's oldest film company still active, 1895). Poetic Realism (1930s), the Nouvelle Vague (1959–), and a state support system (CNC, 1946) that protects French film. Award: the César; festival: Cannes. Tags: #france #french

sections.title: Cinema of Asia (beyond India)
sections.html:
Before you start — MOV-04. Asia makes the majority of the world's films. East Asia's industries (China, Japan, Korea) rival Hollywood at home; South and West Asia have proud old traditions; Southeast Asia is the fastest-growing region.

One of the oldest and most self-sufficient industries, with studios Shochiku, Nikkatsu, Toho (Godzilla, 1954), Daiei and Toei. Golden age of the 1950s: Akira Kurosawa, Yasujirō Ozu, Kenji Mizoguchi, Mikio Naruse. Also anime (Studio Ghibli, Toei Animation), kaiju monster films, J-horror (Ringu, 1998), jidaigeki samurai films. Tags: #japan #japanese #anime

Urdu and Punjabi films centred in Lahore ("Lollywood"), with a golden age in the 1960s, decline in the 1980s–1990s, and revival since Khuda Kay Liye (2007). Pashto films from Peshawar ("Pollywood"), Sindhi films from Karachi. Landmarks: Jago Hua Savera (1959), Bol (2011), The Legend of Maula Jatt (2022, Pakistan's highest-grossing film), Joyland (2022, Cannes Un Certain Regard Jury Prize). Tags: #pakistan #urdu #punjabi #lollywood

  • Bhutan: Khyentse Norbu (The Cup, 1999), Pawo Choyning Dorji (Lunana, Oscar nomination 2022).
  • Afghanistan: Siddiq Barmak's Osama (2003, Golden Globe); filmmakers in exile.
  • Maldives: small Dhivehi-language industry.

Iranian cinema grew from the popular "Film Farsi" before 1979 and the Iranian New Wave (Dariush Mehrjui's The Cow, 1969), and after the revolution produced masters despite censorship: Abbas Kiarostami (Taste of Cherry, Palme d'Or 1997), Mohsen Makhmalbaf, Majid Majidi (Children of Heaven, Oscar nomination), Jafar Panahi (Golden Bear 2015, Palme d'Or 2025 for It Was Just an Accident), Asghar Farhadi (two Oscars: A Separation, The Salesman). Turkish popular cinema of the Yeşilçam era (1950s–1980s), named after a street in Istanbul, made up to about 300 films a year. Masters: Yılmaz Güney (Yol, Palme d'Or 1982), Nuri Bilge Ceylan (Winter Sleep, Palme d'Or 2014), Ferzan Özpetek. Turkish TV dramas (dizi) are now global. Berlin's 2026 Golden Bear went to İlker Çatak's Turkish-language Yellow Letters. Tags: #turkey #turkish

sections.title: Cinema of Africa and Oceania
sections.html:
Before you start — MOV-05. Africa has the world's fastest-growing film culture, from Nollywood's volume to the art cinema of Senegal, Mali and Burkina Faso, and FESPACO, Africa's biggest festival. Oceania adds Australia, New Zealand and Pacific voices.

Algeria's Chronicle of the Years of Fire (1975, Mohammed Lakhdar-Hamina: Palme d'Or, the first for an African film); Tunisia's Moufida Tlatli and the Carthage Film Festival (1966, Africa's and the Arab world's oldest festival); Morocco's Ouarzazate studios, where many Hollywood epics are shot (Egypt: MOV-04.9).

  • Nigeria (Nollywood): born with the home-video drama Living in Bondage (1992, Chris Obi Rapu); now one of the world's largest producers by volume; English, Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa (Kannywood, from Kano) films; landmarks The Wedding Party (2016), Lionheart (2018), King of Boys, A Tribe Called Judah (2023, box-office record). Award: AMVCA and AMAA.
  • Ghana (Ghallywood) and the Twi-language "Kumawood".
  • Senegal: Ousmane Sembène, "father of African cinema" (Black Girl, 1966), Djibril Diop Mambéty (Touki Bouki, 1973), Mati Diop (Atlantics, Cannes Grand Prix 2019; Dahomey, Golden Bear 2024).
  • Mali and Burkina Faso: Souleymane Cissé (Yeelen, 1987, Cannes Jury Prize), Idrissa Ouédraogo; FESPACO in Ouagadougou (1969).
  • Mauritania: Abderrahmane Sissako (Timbuktu, 2014). Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon, Niger.

  • South Africa: Tsotsi (2005, Oscar for Foreign Language Film), District 9 (2009); Cape Town studios.
  • Kenya ("Riverwood"), Tanzania ("Bongo" films), Uganda (Wakaliwood's micro-budget action, Ramon Film Productions), Ethiopia (Haile Gerima), Rwanda, Zimbabwe, Somalia, Sudan (Goodbye Julia, 2023).

  • Australia: The Story of the Kelly Gang (1906), often called the world's first feature-length narrative film; the Australian New Wave of the 1970s (Peter Weir, Picnic at Hanging Rock; George Miller, Mad Max); Baz Luhrmann; Indigenous filmmakers Warwick Thornton, Rachel Perkins; AACTA Awards.
  • New Zealand: Jane Campion (The Piano, Palme d'Or 1993, the first by a woman director), Peter Jackson (The Lord of the Rings, Weta), Taika Waititi; Māori cinema (Whale Rider, 2002).
  • Pacific Islands: Fiji, Samoa, Papua New Guinea, Hawaiian films; Tanna (2015, Vanuatu, Oscar nomination).

Films made by migrant communities between two homelands: Indian diaspora cinema (Mira Nair, Gurinder Chadha's Bend It Like Beckham, Deepa Mehta's Elements Trilogy), Black British cinema, Beur cinema in France, Turkish-German cinema (Fatih Akin), Chinese diaspora films (Crazy Rich Asians), and global co-productions.

The landmark registers above are the trunk. On the website each industry will grow a complete year-wise register in this order: (1) every award-winning and nominated film from the official award databases (MOV-10 to MOV-12); (2) every film in national archives and catalogues (NFAI/NFDC for India, Library of Congress for the USA, BFI for the UK, CNC for France, and their equivalents); (3) every film with an entry in Wikidata (which links to IMDb and national IDs), filtered by country of origin and original language, sorted by year of first release. Each row keeps the same fields as above, plus language, runtime, certificate and streaming availability (dated). Box-office data will come only from named trade sources and will always say gross or net, domestic or worldwide, and the date.

parts.title: Genres, Forms and Formats
parts.intro: About this Part. The second great classification: what kind of film it is. A genre is a family of films that share a promise to the audience (a thriller promises suspense; a comedy promises laughter). Most films belong to more than one genre. Each entry gives one or two lines and example films from different countries, so you can compare India with the world.

sections.title: Film genres and sub-genres
sections.html:
Before you start — MOV-06. Twenty genre families, each with its sub-genres. Use it to find the kind of film you love, then jump to the industries (Part 1) that make it best. See also: BOK genre fiction (shared roots), MUS-film scores.

Films that take real human problems seriously, aiming at emotion and truth more than thrills. Examples: Pather Panchali (India), Tokyo Story (Japan), A Separation (Iran). Tags: #drama

  • Family drama: the joys and fights of families; Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!, Kapoor & Sons, Shoplifters (Japan).
  • Social drama / social problem film: films that question an injustice; Do Bigha Zamin, Article 15, Jai Bhim.
  • Melodrama: heightened emotion, clear good and evil, big music; Mother India, Douglas Sirk's All That Heaven Allows.
  • Coming-of-age: growing up; The 400 Blows, Udaan, Boyhood.
  • Legal and courtroom drama: 12 Angry Men, Jolly LLB, Court, Anatomy of a Fall.
  • Political drama: power and its abuse; Z (Costa-Gavras), Raajneeti, Garm Hava.
  • Medical, sports, workplace and school dramas: Chak De! India, Dangal, Taare Zameen Par, Rocky, Moneyball.
  • Slice-of-life: ordinary days without a big plot; Ozu, Hrishikesh Mukherjee's middle cinema, Paterson.
  • Tragedy: a fall that feels inevitable; Devdas, Kaagaz Ke Phool, Raging Bull.

Films built to make us laugh, from slapstick to satire. Tags: #comedy

  • Slapstick and physical comedy: Chaplin, Keaton, Mehmood, Jagdeep; Andaz Apna Apna.
  • Romantic comedy (rom-com): It Happened One Night, Chupke Chupke, When Harry Met Sally..., Jab We Met.
  • Screwball comedy: fast talk and battles of the sexes (1930s Hollywood).
  • Satire: laughter that attacks folly; Dr. Strangelove, Jaane Bhi Do Yaaro, Peepli Live.
  • Black (dark) comedy: humour about death and crime; Fargo, Delhi Belly, Andhadhun (thriller-comedy).
  • Parody and spoof: Airplane!, Om Shanti Om (homage-parody).
  • Comedy of errors and mistaken identity: Angoor (from Shakespeare), Hera Pheri.
  • Situational and middle-class comedy: Hrishikesh Mukherjee (Golmaal, 1979), Basu Chatterjee.
  • Stand-up and sketch films, mockumentary: This Is Spinal Tap.

Films driven by physical conflict, stunts and spectacle. Tags: #action

  • Martial arts: Enter the Dragon, Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, The Raid.
  • Mass / masala action (India): the hero who defeats fifty men; Baashha, Pokiri, K.G.F, Pushpa.
  • Cop and buddy-cop: Lethal Weapon, Singham, Zanjeer.
  • Heist and caper: Ocean's Eleven, Dhoom, Special 26.
  • Disaster: The Towering Inferno, Titanic (in part), 2018 (Malayalam flood film).
  • Spy and espionage action: James Bond, Mission: Impossible, Ek Tha Tiger, Baby.
  • Superhero: Superman (1978), The Dark Knight, Marvel films, Krrish, Minnal Murali.
  • Gun-fu and "heroic bloodshed": John Woo, John Wick.
  • Car and chase films: Bullitt, Fast & Furious, Mad Max: Fury Road.

Journeys to unknown places, quests and treasure. Raiders of the Lost Ark, Lawrence of Arabia, Life of Pi, Kantara (folk adventure). Sub-genres: swashbuckler (pirates and swords), jungle and survival adventure (The Revenant, Manjummel Boys), lost world, treasure hunt, sea adventure. Tags: #adventure

Films that keep us anxious about what happens next. Tags: #thriller

  • Psychological thriller: Psycho, Black Swan, Raat.
  • Crime thriller: Heat, Drishyam, Vikram Vedha.
  • Political and conspiracy thriller: All the President's Men, Madras Cafe.
  • Erotic thriller, legal thriller, techno-thriller, survival thriller (Buried).
  • Revenge thriller: Oldboy, Kill Bill, Badlapur.
  • Serial-killer and investigative thriller: The Silence of the Lambs, Memories of Murder, Ratsasan.
  • Hitchcockian suspense: the bomb under the table that the audience knows about.

The world of criminals, police and justice. The Godfather, Goodfellas, Nayakan, Satya, Gangs of Wasseypur, City of God, Hong Kong triad films (Infernal Affairs). Sub-genres: film noir (1940s–1950s shadowy crime films: Double Indemnity; neo-noir: Chinatown, Johnny Gaddaar), mafia/underworld, prison films, detective and whodunit (Knives Out, Byomkesh Bakshy!), police procedural. Tags: #crime #noir

Films that make us afraid, and let us enjoy it. Tags: #horror

  • Supernatural and ghost: The Exorcist, Mahal (1949), Bhoot, Ringu.
  • Folk horror: horror rooted in village belief; The Wicker Man, Tumbbad, Bulbbul.
  • Slasher: a masked killer; Halloween, Scream.
  • Monster and creature: Frankenstein, Godzilla, Jaws.
  • Zombie: Night of the Living Dead, Train to Busan, Go Goa Gone (zom-com).
  • Psychological horror: The Shining, Hereditary.
  • Body horror: David Cronenberg, The Substance.
  • Found footage: The Blair Witch Project, Paranormal Activity.
  • Horror-comedy: Stree, Bhool Bhulaiyaa, Shaun of the Dead.
  • Ramsay Brothers horror (India, 1970s–1990s): Purana Mandir, Veerana.
  • J-horror, K-horror, Thai and Indonesian horror: regional schools of fear.

Stories about science, the future, space and "what if". Tags: #scifi

  • Space opera: Star Wars, Dune.
  • Hard science fiction: 2001: A Space Odyssey, Interstellar, The Martian.
  • Dystopian and post-apocalyptic: Metropolis, Blade Runner, Mad Max.
  • Cyberpunk: Blade Runner, Ghost in the Shell, The Matrix.
  • Time travel: Back to the Future, Primer, Aditya 369 (Telugu, 1991), Indru Netru Naalai.
  • Alien contact: Close Encounters of the Third Kind, Arrival, Koi... Mil Gaya, PK.
  • Robots and AI: Ex Machina, Enthiran, Her.
  • Mythological science fiction (India): Kalki 2898 AD.

Magic, myth and impossible worlds. The Wizard of Oz, The Lord of the Rings, Pan's Labyrinth, Spirited Away, Baahubali, Mayabazar. Sub-genres: high/epic fantasy, fairy tale, magical realism (Amélie, Paheli), sword and sorcery, urban fantasy. Tags: #fantasy

Films from the epics, Puranas and saints' lives; the first genre of Indian cinema. Raja Harishchandra, Sant Tukaram, Mayabazar, Jai Santoshi Maa (1975, a surprise blockbuster), Adipurush, Hanu-Man. Also saint films (bhakti biopics), Christian, Islamic and Buddhist religious films worldwide (The Ten Commandments, The Message). Tags: #mythology #devotional #india

Love stories in every shape. Casablanca, Barsaat, Bobby, DDLJ, In the Mood for Love, Premam, 96. Sub-genres: tragic romance (Ek Duuje Ke Liye), romantic drama, period romance, love triangle, star-crossed lovers (Laila–Majnu, Heer–Ranjha films), LGBTQ+ romance (Brokeback Mountain, Call Me by Your Name, Badhaai Do). Tags: #romance

Films in which songs and dance carry the story. Hollywood musicals (Singin' in the Rain, The Sound of Music, La La Land), Indian films (almost all popular Indian films use songs; full musicals like Sangam era dance films, Disco Dancer, ABCD), jukebox musicals (Mamma Mia!), dance films (Saturday Night Fever, Step Up), opera films and concert films. Tags: #musical #dance

Films set in the past. Tags: #history #period

  • Historical epic: Ben-Hur, Mughal-e-Azam, Jodhaa Akbar, Ponniyin Selvan.
  • Biographical (biopic): Gandhi, Bhaag Milkha Bhaag, Oppenheimer, Sardar Udham.
  • Costume drama: Pride & Prejudice, Umrao Jaan.
  • Freedom-struggle films (India): Shaheed (1965), Lagaan, RRR.
  • Partition films: Garm Hava, Tamas, Pinjar, Meghe Dhaka Tara.
  • Samurai (jidaigeki) and wuxia (martial chivalry) period films.

Films about battles, soldiers and the cost of war. All Quiet on the Western Front (1930 and 2022), Saving Private Ryan, Come and See, Haqeeqat (1964), Border, Uri: The Surgical Strike, 1917. Sub-genres: anti-war film, combat film, war epic, home-front drama, Holocaust film (Schindler's List), military biopic (Shershaah). Tags: #war

The American frontier: cowboys, outlaws, sheriffs. Stagecoach, The Searchers, High Noon, Unforgiven. Cousins: the Italian spaghetti Western, India's curry Western and dacoit films (Sholay, Mera Gaon Mera Desh, Paan Singh Tomar), the Australian meat-pie Western, the Ostern (Eastern European and Soviet "Red Westerns"). Tags: #western

Films made frame by frame with drawings, models or computers (also a form: MOV-07.3). Family films (Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, 1937, the first full-length cel-animated feature in colour; Toy Story, 1995, the first fully computer-animated feature), anime, adult animation (Persepolis), stop-motion (Coraline), Indian animation (Hanuman, Mahavatar Narsimha). Tags: #animation

Films made for children or the whole family. E.T., Paddington, Children of Heaven, Makdee, Chillar Party, the Children's Film Society India (CFSI, 1955). Tags: #family #kids

Films around a game or athlete. Rocky, Raging Bull, Chak De! India, Lagaan, Dangal, Iqbal, 83, Ford v Ferrari. Tags: #sports · See also: SPT

Puzzle films that ask "who did it?". Rashomon (truth itself is the mystery), Murder on the Orient Express, Kahaani, Talaash, Satyajit Ray's Feluda films (Sonar Kella). Tags: #mystery

  • Road movie: Easy Rider, Y tu mamá también, Piku, Highway.
  • Survival film: Cast Away, 127 Hours.
  • Mockumentary and pseudo-documentary.
  • Anthology film: several stories in one; Bombay Talkies (2013), Lust Stories, Paris, je t'aime.
  • Hyperlink cinema: crossing storylines; Pulp Fiction, Life in a... Metro, Super Deluxe.
  • Slow cinema: long takes, little plot; Béla Tarr, Lav Diaz, Tsai Ming-liang.
  • Social-media and "screenlife" films: told on screens; Searching (2018), CTRL (2024).
  • Masala film: India's mix-of-all-genres format, serving every rasa in one film (MOV-00.07).

sections.title: Forms, formats and audiences
sections.html:
Before you start — MOV-07. Genre says what a film is about; form says how it is made and shown. See also: MOV-16 Technology.

  • Feature film: over 40 minutes by the Academy's rule (many festivals use 60 minutes or more); typically 90 to 180 minutes.
  • Short film: under about 40 minutes; festival favourite (Clermont-Ferrand).
  • Micro-short and vertical short: under a few minutes, made for phones.

Films about real people and events. Robert Flaherty's Nanook of the North (1922), Dziga Vertov, John Grierson (who coined "documentary" in 1926), cinéma vérité, direct cinema, observational, participatory, essay film (Chris Marker), nature documentary (David Attenborough's series), investigative documentary, docudrama; Indian: Anand Patwardhan, The Elephant Whisperers. Tags: #documentary

Hand-drawn (cel), stop-motion (clay/claymation, puppet, cut-out), computer-generated (3D CGI), rotoscope, motion capture, paint-on-glass, sand animation, pixilation, limited animation (anime), 2.5D. Pioneers: Émile Cohl (Fantasmagorie, 1908), Winsor McCay (Gertie the Dinosaur, 1914), Lotte Reiniger (silhouette feature The Adventures of Prince Achmed, 1926), Ram Mohan ("father of Indian animation").

Films that break story and form: surrealist (Un Chien Andalou, 1929), abstract (Oskar Fischinger, Norman McLaren), structural film, video art, Indian experimental cinema (Mani Kaul, Kumar Shahani, Amit Dutta).

Silent, sound, black-and-white, colour (Technicolor, 1930s), widescreen (CinemaScope, 1953), 3D (1950s craze; Avatar 2009; India's My Dear Kuttichathan, 1984, the first Indian 3D film), IMAX (1970), 70 mm, high frame rate, 4DX, VR cinema, interactive film.

Theatrical, festival, direct-to-video (Nollywood's origin), television film, streaming original (OTT), web series (episodic, a neighbour of film), YouTube cinema.

India's CBFC certificates: U (all), U/A 7+, U/A 13+, U/A 16+ (parental guidance by age, from 2024), A (adults), S (special audiences). USA (MPA): G, PG, PG-13, R, NC-17. UK (BBFC): U, PG, 12A, 15, 18. Each country has its own system (MOV-17.3).

Blockbuster/tentpole, mid-budget, low-budget/independent, micro-budget, B-movie, art-house, crowd-funded (Manthan, 1976, funded by 500,000 farmers paying ₹2 each), co-production.

parts.title: Movements, Schools and Styles
parts.intro: About this Part. A movement is a group of filmmakers in a time and place who share ideas about what cinema should be. Movements are how cinema argues with itself. Listed roughly in order of time.

sections.title: Film movements of the world
sections.html:
Before you start — MOV-08. Read this with Part 1 (where the movements happened) and Part 8 (the theories behind them). See also: MOV-18 Film theory.
  • MOV-08.1 Early cinema "cinema of attractions" (1895–1906): films that showed rather than told: tricks, trains, dances (term by historian Tom Gunning).
  • MOV-08.2 Swedish silent golden age (1917–1924): Victor Sjöström, Mauritz Stiller; nature as emotion.
  • MOV-08.3 German Expressionism (1919–1930s): painted shadows and twisted sets showing inner fear; Caligari, Nosferatu, Metropolis; shaped horror and noir.
  • MOV-08.4 Soviet Montage (1924–1930): meaning made by collision of shots; Eisenstein, Vertov, Pudovkin, Kuleshov.
  • MOV-08.5 French Impressionism and Surrealism (1918–1930): Abel Gance, Germaine Dulac, Luis Buñuel and Salvador Dalí.
  • MOV-08.6 Classical Hollywood style (1917–1960): invisible editing, continuity, star and genre; the "standard" others reacted against.
  • MOV-08.7 Poetic Realism (France, 1930s): doomed lovers in foggy ports; Marcel Carné, Jean Renoir, Jean Vigo.
  • MOV-08.8 Italian Neorealism (1943–1952): real streets, non-actors, poverty after war; Rossellini, De Sica, Visconti; inspired Ray, Bimal Roy and the IPTA films.
  • MOV-08.9 IPTA and the Indian socialist realist films (1940s–1950s): Indian People's Theatre Association artists in cinema; Dharti Ke Lal (1946), Neecha Nagar, K. A. Abbas, Balraj Sahni.
  • MOV-08.10 Japanese golden age (1950s): Kurosawa, Ozu, Mizoguchi.
  • MOV-08.11 Free Cinema and British New Wave (1956–1963): working-class "kitchen sink" realism; Lindsay Anderson, Tony Richardson.
  • MOV-08.12 French New Wave / Nouvelle Vague (1958–1968): critics of Cahiers du cinéma turned directors; jump cuts, location shooting, the director as author; Truffaut, Godard, Rohmer, Rivette, Chabrol, Agnès Varda (Left Bank group).
  • MOV-08.13 Indian Parallel Cinema / New Indian Cinema (1952–1990s): realist, socially engaged, often state-funded; Ray, Ghatak, Sen, then Benegal, Nihalani, Adoor, Aravindan, Mani Kaul, Kumar Shahani, Girish Kasaravalli. Its "middle cinema" cousins: Hrishikesh Mukherjee, Basu Chatterjee, Gulzar.
  • MOV-08.14 Czechoslovak New Wave (1962–1968): absurd humour against censorship; Forman, Chytilová, Menzel.
  • MOV-08.15 Cinema Novo (Brazil, 1960s): "aesthetics of hunger"; Glauber Rocha, Nelson Pereira dos Santos.
  • MOV-08.16 Third Cinema (Latin America, 1969): political, anti-colonial cinema (manifesto by Solanas and Getino, Argentina).
  • MOV-08.17 New Hollywood (1967–1980): young directors, darker stories; Bonnie and Clyde, Taxi Driver.
  • MOV-08.18 New German Cinema (1962–1982): the Oberhausen Manifesto: "Papa's cinema is dead".
  • MOV-08.19 Iranian New Wave (1969–): poetic realism, children and landscapes; Mehrjui, Kiarostami, Makhmalbaf, Panahi.
  • MOV-08.20 Australian New Wave (1970s) and Taiwan New Cinema (1982–).
  • MOV-08.21 China's Fifth Generation (1984–): Yellow Earth, Red Sorghum.
  • MOV-08.22 Hong Kong New Wave (1979–) and heroic bloodshed.
  • MOV-08.23 Cinéma du look (France, 1980s): stylish visuals; Luc Besson, Jean-Jacques Beineix.
  • MOV-08.24 New Queer Cinema (1990s): Todd Haynes, Gregg Araki.
  • MOV-08.25 Dogme 95 (Denmark, 1995): ten rules: handheld camera, real locations, no added music.
  • MOV-08.26 Korean New Wave (late 1990s–): genre-bending, bold violence and class satire.
  • MOV-08.27 Romanian New Wave (2001–): long takes, bureaucratic absurdity.
  • MOV-08.28 Mumblecore (USA, 2000s): micro-budget, naturalistic talk.
  • MOV-08.29 Greek Weird Wave (2009–): absurd, cold, disturbing; Yorgos Lanthimos.
  • MOV-08.30 Malayalam New Generation (2011–) and the new Hindi indie wave: realism, regional texture, strong writing.
  • MOV-08.31 Pan-Indian cinema (2015–): big-budget films released in several languages at once.
  • MOV-08.32 Slow cinema and elevated horror (contemporary tendencies).

parts.title: The History of Cinema: a Timeline
parts.intro: About this Part. The full story in order, with world and Indian events side by side. Every row can become a page on the website.

sections.title: Timeline of world and Indian cinema
sections.html:
Before you start — MOV-09. Read the Introduction twig (Part 0) first for the story; use this timeline for the facts. See also: TEC (camera and sound technology), SNT-02 history of technology.

  • Prehistory: cave paintings with multiple legs suggesting movement; storytelling by firelight.
  • c. 200 BCE–200 CE: Bharata's Natyashastra; Greek theatre; shadow puppetry spreads in Asia.
  • c. 1000 CE: Ibn al-Haytham explains the camera obscura (Book of Optics).
  • 1659: magic lantern (Christiaan Huygens).
  • 1820s–1830s: thaumatrope, phenakistiscope (Joseph Plateau, 1832), zoetrope (1834).
  • 1826–1839: photography: Niépce's first photograph, Daguerre's daguerreotype (1839).
  • 1878: Muybridge's Horse in Motion.
  • 1882: Étienne-Jules Marey's chronophotographic gun.
  • 1888: Le Prince's Roundhay Garden Scene; Eastman's Kodak camera.
  • 1889: celluloid roll film (Eastman).
  • 1891–1894: Edison and Dickson's Kinetograph and Kinetoscope; first Kinetoscope parlour, New York (1894).

  • 1895: Skladanowsky brothers' Bioscop show in Berlin (November); Lumières' Cinématographe screening in Paris (28 December).
  • 1896: Lumière films in Bombay (7 July); cinema reaches every continent.
  • 1899: H. S. Bhatavdekar films a wrestling match (India).
  • 1902: Méliès' A Trip to the Moon; J. F. Madan begins film shows in Calcutta.
  • 1903: The Great Train Robbery.
  • 1905: first nickelodeon, Pittsburgh.
  • 1906: The Story of the Kelly Gang (Australia), early feature-length film.
  • 1907: Elphinstone Bioscope (Madan), early Indian film exhibition chain.
  • 1908: first animated cartoon (Fantasmagorie); Motion Picture Patents Company (USA).

  • 1912–1913: Shree Pundalik (1912); Raja Harishchandra (3 May 1913).
  • 1914: Cabiria; Chaplin's Tramp appears.
  • 1915: The Birth of a Nation.
  • 1918: Indian Cinematograph Act; Keechaka Vadham (South India).
  • 1919–1920: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari; United Artists founded (Chaplin, Pickford, Fairbanks, Griffith).
  • 1922: Nanook of the North; Nosferatu.
  • 1925: Battleship Potemkin; The Gold Rush.
  • 1927: Metropolis; Napoléon; Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences founded; Indian Cinematograph Committee report (1927–28).

  • 1927: The Jazz Singer.
  • 1928: Mickey Mouse in Steamboat Willie (synchronised sound cartoon).
  • 1929: first Academy Awards (16 May).
  • 1931: Alam Ara (14 March); Kalidas (Tamil/Telugu).
  • 1932: first Venice Film Festival, the world's oldest.
  • 1932–1934: Indian studios: Prabhat (1929), New Theatres (1931), Bombay Talkies (1934).
  • 1934: Hollywood's Production Code enforced.
  • 1935: three-strip Technicolor feature Becky Sharp; Devdas (New Theatres).
  • 1937: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs; Kisan Kanya, India's first indigenous colour film (Ardeshir Irani).
  • 1939: Gone with the Wind, The Wizard of Oz; Cannes planned, cancelled by war.
  • 1940–1945: wartime propaganda films; Gemini Studios rises (1940).

  • 1945–1948: Italian Neorealism; Bicycle Thieves.
  • 1946: first Cannes festival; Neecha Nagar shares the Grand Prix.
  • 1948: Paramount decision ends the studio system in the USA.
  • 1950–1951: Rashomon wins at Venice; Berlin festival founded (1951); Central Board of Film Censors (India, 1951); Cinematograph Act 1952.
  • 1952: first International Film Festival of India (Bombay); Calcutta Film Society influence.
  • 1953: CinemaScope (The Robe); 3D boom.
  • 1954: first National Film Awards and first Filmfare Awards (India); Seven Samurai; Godzilla.
  • 1955: Pather Panchali; Children's Film Society India founded.
  • 1957: Mother India; Pyaasa; The Seventh Seal.
  • 1959: French New Wave (The 400 Blows, Breathless 1960).

  • 1960: Mughal-e-Azam; Psycho; La Dolce Vita; Film Institute of India, Pune (FTII).
  • 1962: first James Bond film, Dr. No.
  • 1964: National Film Archive of India founded (Pune).
  • 1968: MPAA ratings replace the Hays Code; 2001: A Space Odyssey.
  • 1969: Film Finance Corporation backs Bhuvan Shome and Uski Roti; Dadasaheb Phalke Award begins (Devika Rani).
  • 1972: The Godfather.
  • 1973: Zanjeer; Enter the Dragon.
  • 1975: Sholay, Deewaar, Jai Santoshi Maa; Jaws; NFDC formed (1975; the FFC merged into it in 1980).

  • 1977: Star Wars; Industrial Light & Magic.
  • 1980s: VHS and the video boom; Doordarshan colour TV in India (1982 Asian Games).
  • 1982: Gandhi (Richard Attenborough), eight Oscars; Bhanu Athaiya becomes the first Indian Oscar winner (1983).
  • 1984: "Betamax case" ruling (USA); My Dear Kuttichathan, India's first 3D film.
  • 1988: Salaam Bombay! wins the Caméra d'Or.
  • 1992: Satyajit Ray's Honorary Oscar; Living in Bondage starts Nollywood; Roja.
  • 1993: Jurassic Park, CGI creatures.
  • 1995: Toy Story, first fully CGI feature; DDLJ; cinema's centenary.

  • 1997: PVR Anupam, India's first multiplex; Titanic.
  • 1998: Indian government grants film "industry" status (formalised 2000–2001), opening bank finance.
  • 1999: The Matrix; The Blair Witch Project; first digital cinema projections.
  • 2001: Lagaan Oscar-nominated; The Lord of the Rings begins; Spirited Away.
  • 2002: Star Wars: Episode II shot fully on digital video.
  • 2007: Netflix starts streaming.
  • 2009: Avatar's 3D; Slumdog Millionaire wins eight Oscars, including two for A. R. Rahman and one each for Resul Pookutty and Gulzar (for lyrics, shared with Rahman).

  • 2012: most US cinemas have converted to digital projection; 35 mm prints are phased out.
  • 2015–2017: Baahubali films; Chinese box office booms.
  • 2016: Netflix and Amazon Prime Video launch in India (Hotstar began in 2015); Netflix reaches 190 countries.
  • 2019: Avengers: Endgame; Parasite (Palme d'Or, then Oscars in 2020).
  • 2020–2021: COVID-19 closes cinemas; direct-to-streaming releases.
  • 2022: RRR; Films Division and other units merged into NFDC; Jeanne Dielman tops Sight and Sound.
  • 2023: "Naatu Naatu" and The Elephant Whisperers win Oscars; WGA and SAG-AFTRA strikes over pay and AI; Cinematograph (Amendment) Act 2023 against piracy.
  • 2024: All We Imagine as Light wins Cannes Grand Prix; CBFC's new age-based U/A categories.
  • 2025: Ne Zha 2 becomes the highest-grossing animated film; Jafar Panahi wins the Palme d'Or.
  • 2026: One Battle After Another wins Best Picture (March); Cristian Mungiu's Fjord wins the Palme d'Or (May); Woman Unknown wins the Golden Lion (September); Avengers: Endgame re-takes the all-time box-office record after a re-release (October). (As checked on 3 November 2026.)
  • The present scenario: streaming and theatres side by side; AI tools on set; regional-language cinema rising; Asia as the growth centre of world box office.

parts.title: Awards, Festivals and Records
parts.intro: About this Part. For each award: what it is, who gives it, how and when it began, its first winner, landmark winners, records and the latest winner, with the date the fact was checked. International awards and festivals come first, then national awards country by country, with India in full. As checked on 3 November 2026. Sources: the official site of each award (Part 13).

sections.title: International film awards
sections.html:
Before you start — MOV-10. "International" here means awards watched by the whole world, even if one country's academy gives them (like the Oscars). See also: MOV-11 Festivals, MOV-13 Records, MOV-14 People.

Given every year by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS, founded 1927) to honour films released in the previous year; voted by about 10,000 film professionals. The gold statuette was designed by Cedric Gibbons and sculpted by George Stanley. Tags: #award #usa #oscars

  • How it began: the first ceremony was a 15-minute dinner at the Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel on 16 May 1929.
  • First winners: Wings (Outstanding Picture) and Sunrise (Unique and Artistic Production); Emil Jannings (Actor) and Janet Gaynor (Actress).
  • Main categories: Picture, Director, Actor, Actress, Supporting roles, Original and Adapted Screenplay, International Feature Film (earlier "Foreign Language Film", from 1956 as a competitive category), Animated Feature (from 2001), Documentary, Cinematography, Editing, Score, Song, Sound, Production Design, Costume, Makeup and Hairstyling, Visual Effects, Short films, Casting (first given at the 98th ceremony, 2026), Honorary awards.
  • Landmark winners: Hattie McDaniel, first Black winner (1940); All About Eve (14 nominations); Sidney Poitier, first Black Best Actor (1964); Parasite (2020), first non-English Best Picture; Kathryn Bigelow, first woman Best Director (2010); Michelle Yeoh, first Asian Best Actress (2023).
  • Records: most wins for a film: 11 (Ben-Hur, Titanic, The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King); most wins for a person: Walt Disney (22 competitive); most acting wins: Katharine Hepburn (4); most nominations for an actor: Meryl Streep (21).
  • India at the Oscars: Bhanu Athaiya (Costume Design, Gandhi, 1983), the first Indian winner; Satyajit Ray (Honorary Award, 1992); A. R. Rahman (two), Resul Pookutty and Gulzar for Slumdog Millionaire (2009); M. M. Keeravani and Chandrabose for "Naatu Naatu" (RRR) and Kartiki Gonsalves and Guneet Monga for The Elephant Whisperers (2023); Indian engineers have also won Scientific and Technical Awards. India's nominations for International Feature: Mother India (1958), Salaam Bombay! (1989), Lagaan (2002).
  • Latest: 98th Academy Awards (15 March 2026): Best Picture One Battle After Another; Director Paul Thomas Anderson; Actor Michael B. Jordan (Sinners); Actress Jessie Buckley (Hamnet); Supporting Actor Sean Penn; Supporting Actress Amy Madigan (Weapons); International Feature Sentimental Value (Norway); Animated Feature KPop Demon Hunters.

The British Academy of Film and Television Arts awards (the academy began in 1947; first film awards in 1949). The mask trophy was designed by Mitzi Cunliffe. First Best Film: The Best Years of Our Lives. Seen as a guide to the Oscars. Latest (22 February 2026): Best Film One Battle After Another, which won six BAFTAs. Tags: #award #uk

Begun in 1944 by the Hollywood Foreign Press Association (dissolved in 2023; the Globes are now run by a private company with an international voting body). Separate Drama and Musical/Comedy categories; also television. First Best Picture: The Song of Bernadette. Latest: see goldenglobes.com (not verified for this edition). Tags: #award #usa

Given by the European Film Academy since 1988 (first Best Film: Krzysztof Kieślowski's A Short Film About Killing). Celebrates European cinema across borders.

Asian Film Awards (Hong Kong, since 2007) and the Asia Pacific Screen Awards (Australia, since 2007) honour films across Asia and the Pacific, including India.

  • FIPRESCI Prize: from the International Federation of Film Critics (founded 1925), given at festivals worldwide.
  • Annie Awards (since 1972): the top awards for animation.
  • Platino Awards (since 2014): Ibero-American (Spanish- and Portuguese-language) cinema.
  • Africa Movie Academy Awards (AMAA) (since 2005) and Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards (AMVCA) (since 2013).
  • Lux Audience Award of the European Parliament.
  • Saturn Awards (science fiction, fantasy, horror, since 1972) and the Golden Raspberry ("Razzies") for the worst films (since 1981).
  • Emmy Awards: for television, not film (included here only to avoid confusion).

sections.title: Film festivals of the world and their top prizes
sections.html:
Before you start — MOV-11. Festivals are where art cinema is discovered and sold. The FIAPF (International Federation of Film Producers Associations) accredits competitive festivals; the most prestigious are called the "Big Three": Cannes, Venice and Berlin.

Held every May on the French Riviera. Planned for 1939 as a free alternative to a Venice festival then influenced by fascist Italy, but cancelled by the Second World War; first held in 1946. Tags: #festival #france #cannes

  • Top prize: the Palme d'Or (from 1955; earlier the Grand Prix). First Palme d'Or: Marty (Delbert Mann, 1955).
  • Other prizes: Grand Prix, Jury Prize, Best Director, Best Actor, Best Actress, Best Screenplay, Caméra d'Or (best first film), Un Certain Regard, Short Film Palme d'Or; parallel sections Directors' Fortnight and Critics' Week.
  • Landmarks: Neecha Nagar shared the first Grand Prix (1946); Jane Campion became the first woman to win (The Piano, 1993, shared); Parasite (2019) was the first Korean winner. Two-time winners include Francis Ford Coppola, Shohei Imamura, Emir Kusturica, Bille August, the Dardenne brothers, Ken Loach, Michael Haneke, Ruben Östlund and Cristian Mungiu.
  • India at Cannes: Neecha Nagar (1946), Do Bigha Zamin (Prix International, 1954), Pather Panchali (Best Human Document, 1956), Kharij (Jury Prize, 1983), Salaam Bombay! (Caméra d'Or, 1988), Marana Simhasanam (Caméra d'Or, 1999), All We Imagine as Light (Grand Prix, 2024), Anasuya Sengupta (Best Actress, Un Certain Regard, 2024, The Shameless).
  • Latest: 79th festival (May 2026): Palme d'Or Fjord (Cristian Mungiu, his second); Grand Prix Minotaur (Andrey Zvyagintsev); Best Director shared by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (La Bola Negra) and Paweł Pawlikowski (Fatherland).

The oldest film festival in the world, first held in 1932 as part of the Venice Biennale, every late August–September on the Lido. Tags: #festival #italy #venice

  • Top prize: the Golden Lion (Leone d'Oro), named in 1949; first winner under that name: Manon (Henri-Georges Clouzot, 1949).
  • Other prizes: Silver Lion (Grand Jury Prize and Best Director), Volpi Cups for acting, Orizzonti section, Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement.
  • Landmarks: Rashomon (1951) introduced Japanese cinema to the West; Satyajit Ray's Aparajito (1957); Mira Nair's Monsoon Wedding (2001); Joker (2019) and Nomadland (2020).
  • Latest: 83rd festival (September 2026): Golden Lion Woman Unknown (Kvinde Ukendt, May el-Toukhy, Denmark); Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize Possible Love (Lee Chang-dong); Volpi Cups to Mathilde Arcel and John Malkovich. (2025: Father Mother Sister Brother, Jim Jarmusch.)

Founded in 1951 in West Berlin, in February; known for political and diverse cinema and the biggest public audience of the Big Three. Tags: #festival #germany #berlin

  • Top prize: the Golden Bear; Silver Bears for direction, performance (gender-neutral since 2021), screenplay and more; the Teddy Award for LGBTQ+ films (1987).
  • India at Berlin: Satyajit Ray won Silver Bears for Best Director (Mahanagar, 1964; Charulata, 1965) and the Golden Bear for Ashani Sanket (1973); Mrinal Sen's Akaler Sandhane (Silver Bear, 1981).
  • Latest: 76th Berlinale (February 2026): Golden Bear Yellow Letters (İlker Çatak). (2025: Dreams (Sex Love), Dag Johan Haugerud; 2024: Dahomey, Mati Diop.)

  • San Sebastián (Spain, 1953): Golden Shell.
  • Locarno (Switzerland, 1946): Golden Leopard; open-air Piazza Grande.
  • Karlovy Vary (Czech Republic, 1946): Crystal Globe.
  • Tokyo International (Japan, 1985): Tokyo Grand Prix.
  • Shanghai International (China, 1993): Golden Goblet.
  • Cairo International (Egypt, 1976): Golden Pyramid; the Arab world's oldest competitive festival accredited by FIAPF.
  • Mar del Plata (Argentina, 1954): Latin America's only FIAPF competitive festival.
  • Tallinn Black Nights (Estonia, 1997) and Warsaw (Poland, 1985).
  • International Film Festival of India (IFFI), Goa (1952): Golden Peacock; FIAPF-accredited competitive festival; Satyajit Ray Lifetime Achievement Award.

  • Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) (Canada, 1976): the People's Choice Award, a famous Oscar predictor.
  • Sundance (USA, 1978; Sundance name 1991): American independent cinema.
  • Telluride (1974) and New York Film Festival (1963).

sections.title: National film awards, country by country
sections.html:
Before you start — MOV-12. Each country honours its own cinema. India comes first and in full; then every region. See also: MOV-01 to MOV-05 (each industry's register lists its award winners).

  • National Film Awards (since 1954): India's highest film honours, given by the President of India; managed today by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting through NFDC (earlier the Directorate of Film Festivals). Golden Lotus (Swarna Kamal) and Silver Lotus (Rajat Kamal) medals. First Best Feature Film: Shyamchi Aai (Marathi). Records: Shabana Azmi, five Best Actress awards; Amitabh Bachchan, four Best Actor awards. Latest verified: 71st National Film Awards (announced 1 August 2025, presented 23 September 2025, for films of 2023): Best Feature Film 12th Fail; Best Actor Shah Rukh Khan (Jawan) and Vikrant Massey (12th Fail); Best Actress Rani Mukerji (Mrs Chatterjee vs Norway).
  • Dadasaheb Phalke Award (since 1969): India's highest honour for lifetime contribution to cinema, given with the National Film Awards. First awardee: Devika Rani. Recent: Mithun Chakraborty (2022 award), Mohanlal (2023 award, presented 2025).
  • Filmfare Awards (since 21 March 1954): the oldest major popular film awards, by Filmfare magazine (Times Group); voted by audience and jury. First Best Film Do Bigha Zamin; first Best Actor Dilip Kumar (Daag); first Best Actress Meena Kumari (Baiju Bawra). Records: Dilip Kumar and Shah Rukh Khan, eight Best Actor awards each. Latest: 70th Filmfare Awards (11 October 2025, Ahmedabad): Best Film Laapataa Ladies (13 awards, equalling Gully Boy's record); Best Actor Abhishek Bachchan and Kartik Aaryan; Best Actress Alia Bhatt (Jigra). Also Filmfare Awards South, Marathi, Bangla, Punjabi and OTT editions.
